description:
Dollarbeg Castle stands in the small Clackmannanshire town of Dollar, and its documented history reaches back further than the imposing Victorian mansion that dominates the site today. The land was granted by King Alexander II to the monks of Dunfermline Abbey in 1236, part of the extensive medieval landholdings that Scottish religious houses accumulated across the country in this period. Ownership eventually passed to the Scotland family, who divided the estate into two separate holdings, Easter and Wester Dollarbeg, and in 1785 the property came into the hands of the 4th Duke of Atholl, connecting Dollarbeg to one of Scotland's most prominent aristocratic families for a period.

The building that gives Dollarbeg Castle its current identity, however, is a considerably later construction. In the 1880s, the estate was purchased by William Henry Dobie, a Victorian railway magnate whose business interests extended to Canada — one of many Scottish fortunes of the period built through the era's rapid expansion of railway infrastructure across the British Empire and beyond. Dobie demolished the older manor house that had stood at Easter Dollarbeg and commissioned an entirely new mansion, built between 1887 and 1889 to a design by Ebenezer Simpson, an architect based in nearby Stirling. Simpson's design, executed in a Victorian Gothic Baronial style, is genuinely notable within Scottish architectural history: it is described as the last building of this particular type ever constructed, marking something of an end point for a style of grand historicist Scottish mansion-building that had flourished for much of the preceding century.

Dollarbeg's 20th-century history moved through some genuinely varied uses. In the 1930s, the mansion's Great Hall hosted social gatherings, functioning as a venue for the kind of formal entertaining typical of substantial country houses in this period. The Second World War brought a far more utilitarian role: the estate served as an RAF radar control station, part of the wider air defence network protecting Britain's skies, a role shared by numerous large country properties requisitioned for military use during the conflict. By the early 2000s, Dollarbeg had been converted for residential and holiday use, split into 10 separate apartments in 2004.

Today Dollarbeg's accommodation model follows the same exclusive-use pattern seen elsewhere in this pilot collection at properties like Aikwood Tower and Faside Estate: rather than booking a single hotel room, guests reserve entire self-contained units within the historic building. The best-known of these is 'The Tower at Dollarbeg Castle,' a luxury three-bedroom apartment spread across the mansion's tower, complete with its own dedicated cinema room and a private rooftop terrace offering panoramic views over the surrounding Ochil Hills countryside; the Great Hall itself is also listed separately as its own distinct retreat. There is no public visiting arrangement of any kind at Dollarbeg — anyone wishing to experience the building needs to book one of these self-contained units as an overnight stay.

Set in Scotland's smallest county, within easy reach of Stirling and the wider central Scotland castle and battlefield landscape, Dollarbeg offers a genuinely unusual combination for visitors seeking self-catering accommodation: the scale and drama of a full Victorian Gothic mansion, broken down into private, self-contained apartments rather than experienced as a single shared hotel.

Dollar itself is best known for Dollar Academy, one of Scotland's most prominent independent schools, and for Castle Campbell, a genuinely medieval fortress perched dramatically in the hills immediately above the town — a striking contrast to Dollarbeg's own Victorian Gothic reinvention of the castle form, and a reminder that this small Clackmannanshire town holds two very different kinds of 'castle' experience within walking distance of each other, from Castle Campbell's genuine 15th-century ruin to Dollarbeg's late-Victorian architectural fantasy.

faqs.question: Can I book a single room at Dollarbeg Castle?
faqs.answer: No. Dollarbeg operates on an exclusive-use, self-catering basis — guests book entire self-contained units within the historic mansion, such as 'The Tower at Dollarbeg Castle,' a three-bedroom apartment with its own cinema room, rather than a single hotel room. There is no public visiting arrangement; the building can only be experienced by booking one of these units as an overnight stay.

faqs.question: Why is Dollarbeg Castle's architecture historically significant?
faqs.answer: The current mansion, built between 1887 and 1889 by Stirling architect Ebenezer Simpson for railway magnate William Henry Dobie, is described as the last building of its particular Victorian Gothic Baronial type ever constructed in Scotland — marking something of an end point for a grand historicist mansion-building style that had flourished throughout much of the 19th century.

faqs.question: What role did Dollarbeg Castle play during the Second World War?
faqs.answer: During the Second World War, Dollarbeg served as an RAF radar control station, part of the wider British air defence network. This followed a more social use in the 1930s, when the mansion's Great Hall hosted formal gatherings, before the building's eventual conversion into 10 separate apartments in 2004.
